equity.level_reason: Disparities by race, income and immigrant status are framed and structural inequities named, but the only group-specific figures (Table 2) are cited from an earlier report, and the article computes no contrast of its own.

level_alternative.reason: Table 2 shows geometric means by race/ethnicity and income side by side, and the Discussion describes these disparities, although the figures are cited.

ev.q: 97.5th percentile of the blood lead distribution in U.S. children aged 1–5 years
geographic, socioeconomic, and racial/ethnic disparities in lead exposure, especially among young children, persist.
children eligible for Medicaid, and children living in areas with higher poverty rates
those who are immigrants or refugees are more likely to live in communities where lead is pervasive.

determinants_of_health.v: structural inequities in the built environment and access to health care; housing built before 1978

ev.q: Their ongoing lead exposure reflects persistent structural inequities in the built environment and access to health care.
These communities often have homes built before 1978, many of which contain lead-based paint.

equity.equity_measurement: Table 2 (cited from a prior report) shows weighted GMs for three race/ethnicity groups only and income-to-poverty ratio dichotomized at 1.3; no contrasts computed.

notes: Policy update; the BLRV of 3.5 μg/dL comes from the LEPAC workgroup's NHANES analysis and Table 2 is cited from reference 8, so the NHANES sampling weights behind it are not the article's own procedure.
view_issues: Text says GM declined to 0.83 μg/dL 'in 2011–2016 (Table 2)', but the 1976–1980 value (15.2) and the ages 6–11 figures are not in Table 2.
